_what: Five image-to-image recipes that were run and kept, and two that were run and failed. Every strength value here is the one that actually produced the paired image in examples/, not a suggested starting point. Seeds are recorded so any of these can be reproduced.
provenance: https://github.com/sjh9714/awesome-krea-2 — 114 generations, 85 kept, all seeds recorded

rule.holds: Geometry is locked. Material is not.
rule.long: Krea 2 image-to-image holds composition, position and spacing very reliably, and does not add or remove objects. What it does not hold is what things are made of. Anything that forces the model to re-derive how a surface behaves — hard light, a new medium that needs different marks — can quietly swap the material while every edge stays exactly where it was.
rule.below: Under ~0.45 the source composition dominates so hard that the instruction barely lands.
rule.above: At 0.72 the model is free enough to invent, and what it invents replaces your subject. See refusals.
rule.measured_on: 5 kept edits, 3 cut ones, 5 out-of-pair generalisation runs, and 2 second-source confirmations

generalisation._what: Every recipe was derived from one image pair. A recipe that only works on the pair it came from is a screenshot, not a recipe, so each was re-run against a source it was not derived from. Two held, two came back partial, one failed. The tiers below are that result, not an estimate. Two of them were then run a second time against another unrelated source, because a use_when inferred from a single failure is a guess wearing the clothes of a measurement. One held and got sharper; the other turned out to be stated too generously and was narrowed.

tiers.holds: Ran on an unrelated source and did what it says.
tiers.partial: Composition held and the instruction landed incompletely or dragged something else with it. Usable, with the caveat stated.
tiers.narrow: Only works on the kind of source it was derived from.
tiers.conditional: Holds on any source that meets a stated precondition, and that precondition was tested on a second unrelated image rather than inferred from one failure.

determinism.measured: Two runs with the same seed, strength, prompt and input bytes returned images that differed on 0 of 1,048,576 pixels.
determinism.so: If a re-run comes back different, the input changed. The usual culprit is a re-encode: feeding a lossy WebP copy of a PNG that an edit was originally made from moved the result by 17.0/255 mean per-pixel — the composition, palette and medium all returned, the brush texture did not.
determinism.practical: Keep the original file if you intend to re-run. Recording the seed is not enough for image-to-image; the seed and the exact input bytes together are what reproduce a generation.

recipes.name: Relight: overcast to hard low sun
recipes.prompt: Relight this {subject}: replace the flat overcast with hard low-angle late afternoon sun from frame right, casting long shadows across the {surface}. Keep the {landmark} placement, horizon line and framing identical.

slots.subject: what is in the photo, e.g. 'coastline'
slots.surface: what the shadows fall on, e.g. 'basalt'
slots.landmark: the thing that must not move, e.g. 'rock'

recipes.verified: Rock placement and horizon held. Shadow direction obeyed.

generalisation.tested_on: an aerial photograph of wet rice terraces
generalisation.held: Every terrace contour stayed in position and the hard low sun and long shadows arrived exactly as asked.
generalisation.drifted: The material changed. Wet paddies and vegetation came back as dry stone amphitheatre steps — the water is gone.
generalisation.why: Hard light forces the model to re-derive how every surface responds, and a surface that read as wet under flat light gets re-rendered as dry under hard light. It was invisible on the coastline this recipe came from because basalt is dry either way.
generalisation.use_when: The subject is already a hard, dry material — rock, concrete, metal, brick. Check the material, not just the composition, before you accept the result.

second_test.result: Held completely. Same stairwell, same skylight, same handrail, same treads, and a hard low sun arriving with a clean diagonal shadow edge down the right wall. The concrete did not move.
second_test.means: The use_when was a hypothesis drawn from one failure. It is now a tested claim: on a hard dry material this recipe holds, and the wet-terrace drift was about the material, not about the recipe.

recipes.example_prompt: Relight this coastline: replace the flat overcast with hard low-angle late afternoon sun from frame right, casting long shadows across the basalt. Keep the rock placement, horizon line and framing identical.

recipes.name: Relight: one light source, everything else into shadow
recipes.changes: light colour, count of sources, falloff
recipes.prompt: Keep this {subject}'s geometry and perspective exactly. Change only the time and mood: {new_light} instead of {old_light}, one light source at {where}, everything nearer falling into shadow.
recipes.verified: Perspective and vanishing point unchanged. Falloff obeyed.

generalisation.held: Composition exact; a warm glow did appear at the far horizon.
generalisation.drifted: The instruction barely landed. 'Everything nearer falling into shadow' did not happen — the foreground stayed evenly lit and the scene is still overcast.
generalisation.why: One light source at the far end is a physically plausible configuration inside a corridor and not outdoors, where the sky is the light source. The recipe was carrying an assumption about enclosure that the prompt never stated.
generalisation.use_when: An enclosure with no competing daylight — corridors, tunnels, windowless rooms. A room with a live window will keep its window.

second_test.tested_on: an attic workshop with a skylight
second_test.result: Half landed. Warm work lamps came on and the corners fell into shadow, and the skylight stayed exactly as bright as before — the daylight it was told to replace was never removed. It also produced two lamps where the prompt said one.
second_test.means: 'Interiors only' was too generous. The corridor this came from has no competing daylight; an attic does. Switching an existing source off is removing something from the scene, and this model does not remove things — the same rule as the object-removal refusal, one level down. The extra lamp is the numeric-constraint limit showing up a third time.

recipes.example_prompt: Keep this corridor's geometry and perspective exactly. Change only the time and mood: warm amber emergency lighting instead of cold fluorescents, one light source at the far end, everything nearer falling into shadow.

recipes.name: Medium: photograph to gouache painting
recipes.prompt: Re-render {subject} as a gouache painting with visible brush texture and chalky opacity. Every {contour} stays in exactly the same position; only the medium changes.

slots.subject: e.g. 'these terraced fields'
slots.contour: the structure that must survive, e.g. 'terrace contour'

recipes.verified: Terrace contours held position through a full medium change.

generalisation.tested_on: an exploded camera diagram, line art
generalisation.held: Real gouache — chalky opaque paint, visible brush marks, flat edges — with every component in position and spacing.
generalisation.why: Works in both directions. Going from line art to continuous tone is the model dropping structure, which is easy; the reverse is what fails. See limits.line_art_sources.

recipes.example_prompt: Re-render these terraced fields as a gouache painting with visible brush texture and chalky opacity. Every terrace contour stays in exactly the same position; only the medium changes.

recipes.name: Palette: recolour without moving a line
recipes.prompt: Recolour this {subject} to a {palette_name} palette — {colour_1}, {colour_2}, {colour_3}. Keep every outline and flat colour field boundary exactly where it is.
recipes.verified: Every keyblock outline and colour-field boundary stayed put.
recipes.note: Naming three concrete colours works. Naming a mood ('make it moodier') drifts.

generalisation.held: All three named colours landed — rust orange rock, deep teal water, pale bone sky — with the geometry exact.
generalisation.drifted: Mild. On a photograph the phrase 'flat colour field boundary' pulls the result slightly toward illustration. Drop that clause when the source is photographic.
generalisation.why: Naming three concrete colours gives the model a target it can hit without re-deriving anything about the surfaces.

recipes.example_prompt: Recolour this woodblock wave to a dusk palette — deep violet water, salmon sky, warm cream foam. Keep every keyblock outline and flat colour field boundary exactly where it is.

recipes.name: Medium: render to cyanotype blueprint
recipes.prompt: Re-render this {subject} as a cyanotype blueprint: white line work on Prussian blue, every {part} in exactly the same position and spacing.
recipes.verified: Every component held its position and spacing across the medium change.
recipes.note: Confirmed on line art and on a flat-subject photograph. Failed to read as a print on an atmospheric landscape. Where the boundary sits is not established — see limits.line_art_sources.

generalisation.held: Every rock held its exact position and the palette went Prussian blue.
generalisation.drifted: No line work at all. The result is a blue-toned photograph, not a blueprint.
generalisation.why: Outlines are content a photograph does not contain, and the model will not invent them any more than it will invent an object you asked it to add.
generalisation.use_when: The source is already line art.

second_test.tested_on: a line-art mandala and, separately, a flat high-contrast portrait
second_test.result: The mandala came back a genuine blueprint-form cyanotype with every petal in place. The portrait (seed 2026012845) came back a genuine photographic cyanotype print — paper fibre, uneven chemical staining, wash at the edges — with the face exactly preserved.
second_test.means: This falsifies the 'needs a line-art source' rule that was shipped here off a single failure. A photograph can come back as a real cyanotype. What has NOT been established is why the coastline did not: it is the lower-contrast image on the numbers (source std 74.7 against the portrait's 60.4, so contrast is not it), and the visible difference is that the coastline is a deep atmospheric scene while both successes are flat subjects. That is one image per side and it is not enough to state as a rule.

recipes.example_prompt: Re-render this exploded camera diagram as a cyanotype blueprint: white line work on Prussian blue, every component in exactly the same position and spacing.

line_art_sources.finding: WITHDRAWN. This said a cyanotype conversion needs a source that is already line art. A flat high-contrast portrait disproved it.
what_is_actually_known: Line art converts to a blueprint-form cyanotype cleanly (mandala, seed 1507257657).
A flat photographic subject converts to a photographic cyanotype print cleanly (portrait, seed 2026012845).
An atmospheric landscape came back as a blue tint rather than a print (coastline, seed 2065751023).
line_art_sources.not_established: Why the third one differs. Contrast was measured and runs the wrong way. Flatness of the subject is the visible difference and is one observation per side, which is a hypothesis, not a finding. Run it on more sources before trusting either reading.
line_art_sources.rule_of_thumb: Try it. Look at whether the result has paper texture and an uneven wash, or is merely blue.

material_drift.finding: Geometry is the thing that holds. Material is not.
seen_in: relight-hard-sun on wet rice terraces returned dry stone with every contour in place
material_drift.rule_of_thumb: The more a change forces the model to re-derive how a surface behaves, the more the material moves. Palette and continuous-tone medium changes are safe. Hard relighting is not. Check what things are made of in the output, not just where they are.

cannot_switch_off_an_existing_source.finding: Relighting adds light. It does not take light away.

tested.asked: a single warm work lamp instead of flat daylight from the skylight
tested.got: The lamp arrived. The skylight stayed exactly as bright.

cannot_switch_off_an_existing_source.why: An existing light source is content. Turning it off is removal, and removal is the thing this model will not do — see the no-object-removal refusal.
cannot_switch_off_an_existing_source.rule_of_thumb: You can add a source and darken what is away from it. You cannot switch off what is already lit.

refusals.verdict: Krea 2 does not add or remove objects. Refuse and say why.

evidence.asked: Remove the steam entirely and let the coffee surface go still and mirror-flat.

also_failed: Adding snow and sea ice to a coastline returned the same coastline, slightly cooler.
Darkening a sky returned the same sky.
refusals.instead: Use an inpainting model with a mask. This is a segmentation problem, not a strength problem.

refusals.verdict: The same person cannot be carried into a new photograph. Refuse and say why.

evidence.asked: The same woman, now lit only by a laptop screen. Same silver crop, same scar, same wire frames. Identity must be unmistakably the same person.
evidence.got: A new scene with a different person. Only the sweater and the palette carried over.

refusals.why_no_setting_works: 0.45 keeps the face but drags the source composition with it — a three-view studio sheet became the same three views at a harbour. 0.72 gives a genuinely new scene and a different person. There is no value between them that gives you one without the other.
refusals.instead: Train a LoRA. Prompting cannot do this.
